WITNESSES ALSO REPORTED THAT THE AIRPLANE'S ENGINE QUIT RUNNING BEFORE IT STARTED TO LOSE ALTITUDE. WITNESSES STATED THAT THE AIRPLANE THEN BANKED TO THE LEFT, AND THEN OBSERVED THE WINGS "GO VERTICAL" BEFORE GOING STRAIGHT DOWN. THE AIRCRAFT IMPACTED THE FRONT OF A RESIDENTIAL HOUSE ON A MAGNETIC HEADING OF APPROXIMATELY 135 DEGREES. THE PLANE SUBSEQUENTLY CAME TO REST ON THE FRONT PORCH OF THE HOUSE ON A MAGNETIC HEADING OF 090 DEGREES. THERE WAS NO POST-CRASH FIRE. ON AUGUST 30, 2004, A POST-ACCIDENT ON-SITE EXAMINATION BY THE NATIONAL TRANSPORTATION SAFETY BOARD (NTSB) INVESTIGATOR-IN-CHARGE (IIC), A FEDERAL AVIATION ADMINISTRATION (FAA) INSPECTOR (IIC), AND A REPRESENTATIVE OF TELEDYNE CONTINENTAL MOTORS WAS PERFORMED. THE EXAMINATION REVEALED THAT THE COCKPIT AND RIGHT WING WERE DESTROYED, AND ALSO, THAT THE LEFT TIP (FUEL) TANK AND THE RIGHT MAIN FUEL TANK WERE BREACHED, WHILE THE RIGHT TIP TANK, LEFT MAIN FUEL TANK, AND CENTER AUXILIARY FUEL TANK WERE INTACT. BOTH MAIN LANDING AND THE NOSE LANDING GEARS WERE IN THE DOWN AND LOCKED POSITION, AND BOTH WING FLAPS WERE PARTIALLY EXTENDED. THE AIRCRAFT'S ENGINE HAD SEPARATED FROM THE AIRCRAFT AND WAS LOCATED 9 FEET FORWARD AND 20 DEGREES TO THE RIGHT OF THE AIRPLANE'S COCKPIT, INSIDE THE HOUSE. AT APPROXIMATELY 100 MDT, ON AUGUST 30, 2004, THE AIRCRAFT WAS REMOVED FROM THE HOUSE AND TRANSPORTED TO A LOCAL HANGAR (S27) FOR FURTHER EXAMINATION BY THE NTSB, THE FAA INSPECTOR, AND THE TELEDYNE CONTINENTAL MOTOR REPRESENTATIVE. THE EXAMINATION OF THE AIRCRAFT AND THE ENGINE AND THE REMAINING FUEL FOUND ONBOARD WERE INSPECTED. THE REMAINING FUEL OUT OF THE THREE INTACT FUEL TANKS WAS APPROXIMATELY 7 TO 8 GALLONS. THE AIRFRAME WAS INSPECTED AND FOUND TO HAVE BEEN IN AN AIRWORTHY CONDITION BEFORE THE ACCIDENT. THE ONLY SIGNIFICANT THING FOUND WAS THE POSITION OF THE FUEL SELECTOR VALVE, WHICH WAS FOUND TO BE SELECTED PART WAY BETWEEN THE LEFT AND RIGHT MAIN TANKS. THE FUEL SELECTOR VALVE WAS REMOVED AND EXAMINED, AND FOUND TO FUNCTION NORMALLY THROUGH THE DETENTS. COMPONENTS WERE REMOVED FROM THE AIRCRAFT'S ENGINE, THE FUEL PUMP, CARBURETOR, AND MAGNETOS, FOR FURTHER EXAMINATION AND TESTING. THE RESULTS LATER DETERMINED THAT THERE WAS NO MECHANICAL MALFUNCTION OF THE ENGINE COMPONENTS. THE NTSB INSPECTOR AND THE FAA INSPECTOR HAVE CONCLUDED THAT THE PROBABLE CAUSE OF THE ACCIDENT WAS FUEL STARVATION DUE TO MISMANAGEMENT OF FUEL AND THE FUEL SELECTOR VALVE. THIS ACCIDENTIS CONSIDERED CLOSED.

SALT LAKE CITY-AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL TOWER (SLC-ATCT) ATTEMPTED TO VECTOR THE AIRCRAFT FOR AN IFR APPROACH AND LANDING ON RUNWAY 17 AT KSLC. THE PILOT REPORTED UNABLE TO MAINTAIN ALTITUDE AND REQUESTED AN IMMEDIATE APPROACH CLEARANCE. SUBSEQUENTLY THE PILOT REPORTED UNABLE TO RECEIVE THE LOCALIZER FREQUENCY. SOME TIME FOLLOWING THE PILOT REPORTED ABLE TO MAINTAIN ALTITUDE AND REQUESTED CLEARANCE TO THE NEAREST AIRPORT THAT WAS REPORTING            VISUAL METEOROLOGICAL CONDITIONS. SLC-ATCT INFORMED HIM THAT WOULD BE PROVO, UTAH. THE PILOT THEN REQUESTED VECTOR CLEARANCE TO THE AIRPORT AT PROVO (PVU). SLC-ATCT CALLED THE PILOT'S ATTENTION TO THE FACT THAT HE WAS NOT FLYING HIS ASSIGNED HEADING. THE PILOT REPORTED THAT THE AIRCRAFT'S INSTRUMENTS INDICATED THAT HE WAS ON THE CORRECT HEADING. THERE MAY HAVE BEEN A PROBLEM WITH THE ACCURACY OF THE AIRCRAFT'S HORIZONTAL SITUATION INDICATOR (HSI) AS WELL. UPON LANDING AT PROVO, THE PILOT MADE A VISUAL INSPECTION OF THE AIRCRAFT TO DETERMINE THE DAMAGE. WHEN HE TALKED TO ME, HE INFORMED ME THERE WERE SEVERAL AREAS OF DAMAGE: A METAL OBJECT IMPACTED THE LEADING EDGE OF THE RIGHT WING IN BETWEEN THE ENGINE NACELLE AND THE FUSELAGE, THERE WERE SOME HOLES IN THE FUSELAGE ON THE RIGHT SIDE NEAR THE NOSE, CORNERS MISSING FROM TWO BLADES OF THE RIGHT (STARBOARD) PROPELLER, AND A SLICE IN THE LEADING EDGE OF THE STARBOARD HORIZONTAL STABILIZER. THE PILOT TOLD ME THAT HE SHUT THE RIGHT ENGINE DOWN FOR A BRIEF PERIOD OF TIME BECAUSE THE AIRPLANE WAS VIBRATING SO SEVERELY. IT WAS AT THIS TIME THAT HE REPORTED BEING UNABLE TO HOLD ALTITUDE. HE SAID THAT HE TROUBLE SHOT THE SITUATION AND THEN DECIDED TO RESTART THE ENGINE TO MAINTAIN ALTITUDE. AT THIS TIME HE THEN PROCEEDED TO PROVO. HE WAS NOT SURE WHAT HE HIT. SUBSEQUENTLY, SALT LAKE CITY AIRPORT AUTHORITY (SLCAA) CONDUCTED A SEARCH ALONG RUNWAY 35 AND DISCOVERED THE OBJECT THAT WAS HIT. IT WAS AN UNUSED ANTENNA OWNED BY THE NATIONAL WEATHER SERVICE (NWS). SLCAA SAID THE HEIGHT OF THE ANTENNA WAS LESS THAN 100 FEET ABOVE GROUND LEVEL (AGL). THE FOLLOWING MORNING I MET THE PILOT AT PROVO TO CONDUCT AN IN-PERSON INTERVIEW AND A VISUAL INSPECTION OF THE AIRCRAFT. MY VISUAL INSPECTION OF THE AIRPLANE CONFIRMED WHAT THE PILOT TOLD ME OVER THE TELEPHONE THE PREVIOUS NIGHT. THE ACCIDENT PACKAGE FROM SLC-ATCT DIDN'T ARRIVE AT MY OFFICE UNTIL FEBRUARY 25, 2005. THE PILOT TOLD ME DURING THE INTERVIEW THAT METEOROLOGICAL CONDITIONS PRIOR TO TAKEOFF WERE LESS THAN THAT REQUIRED FOR A NORMAL INSTRUMENT LANDING SYSTEM (ILS) APPROACH AND LANDING. HOWEVER, JUST BEFORE TAKEOFF THE VISIBILITY REACHED THE INSTRUMENT FLIGHT RULES (IFR) LANDING MINIMUMS OF 1/2 MILE. AT THE TIME OF THE INTERVIEW, IT NEVER OCCURRED TO ME THAT THE PILOT WAS OCCUPYING THE RIGHT SEAT WHICH IS NORMALLY THE COPILOT'S SEAT. I LEARNED THIS FACT AFTER TALKING TO THE NTSB 2 TO 3 WEEKS LATER AFTER HE INCLUDED THAT FACT IN HIS REPORT TO THEM. THIS IS A FINAL REPORT.
